question: A newly elected mayor was charged with tax fraud. The prosecutor served a trial subpoena directing the mayor's attorney to produce private bank records that the mayor delivered to the attorney. The attorney refused the request. The prosecutor in a hearing then sought to compel compliance with the subpoena. The court should

options.A: compel production, because it would not violate the attorney-client privilege.
options.B: compel production, because the mayor has waived his rights to attorney-client privilege by delivering the records to his attorney.
options.C: not compel production, because it would violate the mayor's privilege against self- incrimination.
options.D: not compel production, because it would violate the attorney-client privilege.
options.E: compel production, because the attorney-client privilege does not extend to financial records.
options.F: not compel production, because the subpoena was not properly served.
options.G: not compel production, because the mayor's financial records are not relevant to the case.
options.H: compel production, because the mayor's financial records could be crucial evidence in the trial.
options.I: not compel production, because it would infringe on the mayor's right to privacy.
options.J: compel production, because there is no element of confidentiality.
